level.title: Scaling & Security
level.description: Handle millions of users without crashing — and without getting hacked. Scaling, load balancing, IAM, least privilege and secrets.

quiz_data.question: What is vertical scaling?
options: Upgrading one server to more CPU and RAM

quiz_data.question: Why is horizontal scaling preferred in the cloud?
options: It is the only option on Linux
There is no hard size limit and one failed server doesn't take the app down

quiz_data.question: What does a load balancer do?
options: Distributes incoming traffic across healthy servers

quiz_data.question: What is the principle of least privilege?
options: Give everyone admin access to save time
Only senior engineers can log in
Give each user or service only the permissions it needs

quiz_data.question: Where should an API key for your app live?
options: In a secrets manager or environment variables — never committed to git

lessons.title: Horizontal vs. Vertical Scaling
lessons.content_md:
# Horizontal vs. Vertical Scaling ⚖️

If your website becomes incredibly popular overnight, your single server won't be able to handle all the traffic. It will crash under the pressure. You need to **Scale** (grow) your app.

There are two ways to do this:

## 1. Vertical Scaling (Scaling UP) 🏢
Imagine you have a small delivery van. Vertical scaling is like taking that van to a mechanic, stripping out the engine, and replacing it with a massive, turbo-charged monster engine. 

In the Cloud, this means keeping your **one server**, but upgrading it to have more CPU and RAM. 
- **The Problem:** A server can only get so big before you hit the physical limits of hardware. Plus, you have to turn the server off to upgrade it!

## 2. Horizontal Scaling (Scaling OUT) 🚗🚗🚗
Imagine you have a small delivery van. Instead of making it bigger, you just buy **10 more identical vans**. 

In the Cloud, this means keeping your small servers, but adding **hundreds of identical copies** of them side-by-side.
- **The Benefit:** There is no limit! If you need more power, you just add another server. This is the true power of the Cloud.

<flipcard front="🏢 What is the difference between Vertical and Horizontal scaling?" back="Vertical (Scaling UP) is making a single server bigger and stronger. Horizontal (Scaling OUT) is adding many more identical servers to share the load."></flipcard>

lessons.title: The Load Balancer: The Traffic Cop
lessons.content_md:
# The Load Balancer: The Traffic Cop 👮‍♂️

So, you chose **Horizontal Scaling**. You now have 5 identical web servers running your app.

When a user types your website address into their browser, which of the 5 servers do they connect to?

If all the users accidentally connect to Server #1, it will crash, while the other 4 servers sit around doing nothing!

## Enter the Load Balancer

To fix this, we put a **Load Balancer** in front of the servers. 

Think of a Load Balancer as a traffic cop standing at a massive intersection during rush hour.
- Car 1 arrives: The cop points them to Server A.
- Car 2 arrives: The cop points them to Server B.
- Car 3 arrives: The cop points them to Server C.

The Load Balancer ensures that the traffic is perfectly distributed so that no single server ever gets overwhelmed.

<flipcard front="👮‍♂️ What is the job of a Load Balancer?" back="A Load Balancer acts like a traffic cop, distributing incoming internet traffic evenly across multiple servers so no single server gets overloaded and crashes."></flipcard>

lessons.title: Cloud Security: IAM, Least Privilege & Secrets
lessons.content_md:
# Cloud Security: IAM, Least Privilege & Secrets 🔐

Scaling gets you more users — and more attackers. Most cloud breaches aren't clever hacks; they're **misconfigurations**: over-powerful credentials, public buckets and leaked keys.

## The Shared Responsibility Model

| The cloud provider secures… | You secure… |
|-----------------------------|-------------|
| Physical data centres | Who can access what (IAM) |
| Hardware and the network backbone | Your data and its encryption settings |
| The managed services themselves | Your code, OS patches (on VMs) and configuration |

<flipcard front="🤝 What is the shared responsibility model?" back="The provider secures the cloud itself (buildings, hardware, core services); you secure what you put in it — identities, permissions, data and configuration."></flipcard>

## Identity & Access Management (IAM)

IAM answers: **who** (a user, group or service) can do **what** (actions) on **which** resource.

```json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Action": ["s3:GetObject"],
    "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::flybeta-avatars/*"
  }]
}
```

This policy only lets its holder **read** objects in **one** bucket — nothing else.

## The Principle of Least Privilege

Give every user and service **only the permissions it needs, and nothing more**.

| ❌ Risky | ✅ Least privilege |
|---------|-------------------|
| App server uses an admin key | App server has a role that can only read one bucket |
| Everyone shares one root login | Individual users, MFA on, root locked away |
| Long-lived access keys on laptops | Short-lived credentials from roles |

<flipcard front="🗝️ What is the principle of least privilege?" back="Grant each user or service only the permissions required for its job — so a leaked credential or a bug can do as little damage as possible."></flipcard>

## Secrets Management

API keys and database passwords must **never** be committed to git or baked into images.

- Store them in a **secrets manager** (AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager, Azure Key Vault).
- Inject them at runtime as environment variables.
- **Rotate** them regularly — and immediately if one leaks.

## Encryption

- **In transit:** HTTPS/TLS everywhere, including between internal services.
- **At rest:** turn on encryption for disks, buckets and databases (usually one setting).

## Quick Security Checklist

- [ ] MFA on every human account; root/owner account locked away
- [ ] No public buckets unless they truly host public files
- [ ] Security groups only open the ports you need (e.g. 443, not 0–65535)
- [ ] Secrets in a secrets manager, never in code
- [ ] Logging of who did what (CloudTrail / Cloud Audit Logs) switched on

lessons.title: Hands-On: Auto Scaling Behind a Load Balancer
lessons.content_md:
# Hands-On: Auto Scaling Behind a Load Balancer 📈

Let's put horizontal scaling and a load balancer together using Docker Compose on your own machine, then see how the cloud automates the same idea.

## 1. A Tiny Service That Reports Who Answered

```python
# app.py
import socket
from flask import Flask
app = Flask(__name__)

@app.get("/")
def hello():
    return {"served_by": socket.gethostname()}
```

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
RUN pip install flask gunicorn
COPY app.py .
CMD ["gunicorn", "-b", "0.0.0.0:8000", "app:app"]
```

## 2. An Nginx Load Balancer

```nginx
# nginx.conf
events {}
http {
  upstream app_servers {
    server app:8000;   # Docker's DNS returns every replica of "app"
  }
  server {
    listen 80;
    location / { proxy_pass http://app_servers; }
  }
}
```

```yaml
# docker-compose.yml
services:
  app:
    build: .
  lb:
    image: nginx:alpine
    ports: ["8080:80"]
    volumes: ["./nginx.conf:/etc/nginx/nginx.conf:ro"]
    depends_on: [app]
```

## 3. Scale Out

```bash
docker compose up --build --scale app=3 -d
for i in 1 2 3 4 5 6; do curl -s localhost:8080; echo; done
```

You'll see `served_by` change between the three containers — the load balancer is spreading requests across them. (Nginx resolves the replicas when it starts, so restart `lb` after scaling up or down.)

## 4. How the Cloud Automates This

| Piece | AWS | GCP | Azure |
|-------|-----|-----|-------|
| Group of identical servers | Auto Scaling Group | Managed Instance Group | VM Scale Set |
| Load balancer | Application Load Balancer | Cloud Load Balancing | Azure Load Balancer |
| Scaling rule | e.g. keep average CPU at 60% | Same idea | Same idea |

The load balancer runs **health checks** and stops sending traffic to unhealthy servers; the scaling group replaces them automatically.

## 5. Challenges

- Kill one container (`docker kill <id>`) and keep curling. What happens?
- Add a `/slow` endpoint that sleeps for 2 seconds and compare 1 vs 3 replicas under load (try `hey` or `ab`).
